lessons.title: What is Sikhism?
lessons.summary: An introduction to Sikhi — its origins, its Gurus and its scripture.

sections.heading: Origins
paragraphs: Sikhism (Sikhi) began in the Punjab region of South Asia with Guru Nanak Dev Ji (1469–1539) and was shaped over two centuries by the ten Gurus. Today it is one of the world's major religions, with an estimated 25–30 million followers worldwide.
The word “Sikh” means learner or disciple. A Sikh is a lifelong student of the Guru's teachings.

sections.heading: The Guru today
paragraphs: Since 1708 the eternal Guru of the Sikhs has been the Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, which contains the words of six of the Gurus alongside saints from different faiths and social backgrounds.

sections.heading: In daily life
list: Remembering the Creator (Naam Japna)
Earning honestly (Kirat Karni)
Sharing with others (Vand Chhakna)
Serving without expectation (Seva)
Treating every person as equal

lessons.title: Core beliefs
lessons.summary: The central beliefs that shape Sikh life.

sections.heading: What Sikhs believe
list: There is One Creator, present in all of creation
The Ten Gurus carried one divine light and message
The Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji is the eternal Guru
All human beings are equal, whatever their caste, gender or background
Liberation is found through remembrance, truthful living and grace — not through ritual

sections.heading: What Sikhi rejects
paragraphs: The Gurus taught against caste discrimination, idol worship, superstition and empty ritual, and against renouncing the world. A Sikh lives as a householder, engaged with family and society.

lessons.title: One God, One Creator
lessons.summary: Sikhi teaches belief in one Creator, beyond form, time and fear.

sections.heading: The Creator in Sikhi
paragraphs: The Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji opens with the Mool Mantar, which describes the Creator as one, eternal truth, the creator of all, without fear or enmity, timeless, beyond birth and self-existent, realised through the Guru's grace.
God is not limited to any one religion or place. The Creator is both beyond creation and present within it — within every person.

sections.heading: Names for God
paragraphs: Sikhs most often use “Waheguru” (Wondrous Enlightener). Gurbani also uses many names drawn from different traditions, such as Ram, Hari, Gobind and Allah, all pointing to the same One.

lessons.title: Equality
lessons.summary: Every person carries the same divine light, so no one is high or low by birth.

sections.heading: Equality in practice
list: In the Langar everyone sits together on the floor and eats the same food
The Gurdwara is open to people of every faith and background
Women and men have equal standing in religious life
The names Singh and Kaur removed caste-based surnames

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: At a time of rigid caste divisions, the Gurus built institutions that made equality visible. The Guru Granth Sahib Ji itself includes the words of saints from so-called “low” castes and from Muslim backgrounds.

lessons.title: Naam Japna
lessons.summary: The first of the three pillars: keeping the Creator in constant remembrance.

sections.heading: Meaning
paragraphs: Naam Japna means remembering and meditating on the Creator's Name — through recitation of Gurbani, Kirtan and quiet meditation on Waheguru — until remembrance becomes part of every moment.

sections.heading: How Sikhs practise it
list: Daily Nitnem
Simran (meditation) on Waheguru
Singing and listening to Kirtan
Keeping the Creator in mind during work and rest

lessons.title: Kirat Karni — honest living
lessons.summary: The second pillar: earning a living honestly through one's own effort.

sections.heading: Meaning
paragraphs: Kirat Karni means working hard and earning truthfully, without cheating or exploiting others. Guru Nanak Dev Ji himself farmed at Kartarpur, showing that spiritual life and honest work go together.

sections.heading: In practice
list: Honest work of any kind is honourable
Avoid deceit, bribery and exploitation
Live as a householder rather than renouncing the world

lessons.title: Vand Chhakna — sharing with others
lessons.summary: The third pillar: sharing one's earnings and blessings with others.

sections.heading: Meaning
paragraphs: Vand Chhakna means sharing what one has — food, time and wealth — especially with those in need. Many Sikhs give Dasvandh, a tenth of their earnings, for community and charitable work.

sections.heading: In practice
list: Contributing to the Langar
Giving Dasvandh
Helping anyone in need, regardless of background

lessons.title: Ik Onkar
lessons.summary: “There is One Creator” — the first words of the Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji.

sections.heading: Meaning
paragraphs: ੴ (Ik Onkar) combines the numeral one (੧) with Oankar, the Creator who is present throughout creation. It is the opening of the Mool Mantar and of the Guru Granth Sahib Ji.
Ik Onkar expresses the oneness of the Creator and of creation: the same light is present in every being.

lessons.title: Naam
lessons.summary: The divine presence that pervades creation, and remembrance of it.

sections.heading: Meaning
paragraphs: Naam, literally “Name”, refers to the Creator's presence that sustains all things. To be attuned to Naam is to live in awareness of the Creator. Gurbani describes Naam as the source of peace and the remedy for ego.

lessons.title: Seva
lessons.summary: Selfless service performed without expectation of reward.

sections.heading: Meaning
paragraphs: Seva is service offered humbly, for others and for the Guru, without seeking praise or reward. It helps a Sikh overcome ego (haumai).

sections.heading: Forms of Seva
list: Cooking and serving in the Langar
Cleaning the Gurdwara and looking after shoes
Helping in disasters and emergencies
Sharing skills and time with the community

lessons.title: Simran
lessons.summary: Meditative remembrance of the Creator.

sections.heading: Meaning
paragraphs: Simran is focused, loving remembrance of the Creator — often by repeating “Waheguru” — so that the mind becomes still and attuned to Naam.

sections.heading: In practice
list: Simran at Amrit Vela (early morning)
Collective Simran in the Sangat
Remembering Waheguru throughout the day

lessons.title: Sangat
lessons.summary: The holy congregation — gathering together in the Guru's presence.

sections.heading: Meaning
paragraphs: Sangat is the community that gathers to sing, listen to and reflect on Gurbani. Gurbani praises the company of the holy (Sadh Sangat) as a place where the mind is uplifted.

sections.heading: In practice
list: Attending the Gurdwara with family and friends
Joining Kirtan and Katha
Supporting one another in Seva

lessons.title: Pangat
lessons.summary: Sitting in a row to eat together as equals in the Langar.

sections.heading: Meaning
paragraphs: Pangat means sitting together in rows to share food. Guru Amar Das Ji asked that all visitors first sit together in the Langar before meeting the Guru, so that no distinction of status or caste remained.

lessons.title: Hukam
lessons.summary: The Divine Order that governs all creation.

sections.heading: Meaning
paragraphs: Hukam is the Creator's will and order, through which everything comes into being. Japji Sahib teaches that by understanding and walking in Hukam, the wall of ego falls away.
Accepting Hukam is not passivity: Sikhs act with effort and courage, while accepting outcomes with humility.

lessons.title: Chardi Kala
lessons.summary: Ever-rising spirits — optimism and resilience in every circumstance.

sections.heading: Meaning
paragraphs: Chardi Kala describes a spirit of eternal optimism rooted in faith. Sikh history is full of examples of people who remained in Chardi Kala through great suffering.

lessons.title: Sarbat da Bhala
lessons.summary: The wellbeing of all — the closing wish of the Sikh Ardas.

sections.heading: Meaning
paragraphs: Sarbat da Bhala means “the welfare of all”. The Sikh Ardas ends by asking for the wellbeing of all humanity, not only of Sikhs — a reminder that a Sikh's concern extends to everyone.

lessons.title: The Five Ks
lessons.summary: The five articles of faith kept by initiated Sikhs.

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Guru Gobind Singh Ji gave the Five Ks (Panj Kakaar) to the Khalsa in 1699. Each begins with the Gurmukhi letter ਕ (K) and together they express commitment, discipline and identity.
list: Kesh — uncut hair
Kangha — wooden comb
Kara — steel bracelet
Kachera — cotton undergarment
Kirpan — article of faith in the form of a sword

lessons.title: Nitnem
lessons.summary: The daily prayers recited morning, evening and night.

sections.heading: The daily Banis
list: Morning: Japji Sahib, Jaap Sahib, Tav-Prasad Savaiye (many also recite Benti Chaupai and Anand Sahib)
Evening: Rehras Sahib
Night: Sohila Sahib (Kirtan Sohila)

sections.heading: Read along
paragraphs: You can read every Nitnem Bani with meanings and audio on the Nitnem page, and track your daily checklist there.

lessons.title: Ardas
lessons.summary: The formal Sikh prayer of supplication, offered standing.

sections.heading: About Ardas
paragraphs: Ardas is recited standing, with hands joined, at the end of services, before undertaking tasks and at important moments. It remembers the Gurus, the sacrifices of Sikhs throughout history and asks for the Guru's grace.
Ardas closes with the wish for Sarbat da Bhala — the wellbeing of all.

lessons.title: Kirtan
lessons.summary: Singing Gurbani to music, in the Raags of the Guru Granth Sahib Ji.

sections.heading: About Kirtan
paragraphs: Kirtan is the singing of Gurbani, usually with harmonium and tabla. Most of the Guru Granth Sahib Ji is arranged in Raags (musical measures), reflecting the central place of music in Sikh worship.

lessons.title: Langar
lessons.summary: The free community kitchen found in every Gurdwara.

sections.heading: About Langar
paragraphs: Langar was begun by Guru Nanak Dev Ji and strengthened by the later Gurus. Volunteers prepare and serve free vegetarian food to anyone who comes, regardless of religion, caste or status.

sections.heading: What it teaches
list: Equality — all sit together (Pangat)
Seva — food is prepared and served by volunteers
Vand Chhakna — the community shares its resources

lessons.title: Gurdwara etiquette
lessons.summary: How to visit a Gurdwara respectfully — everyone is welcome.

sections.heading: When you visit
list: Cover your head; head coverings are usually available
Remove your shoes and wash your hands
Do not bring tobacco, alcohol or other intoxicants
Bow or sit quietly before the Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, and sit on the floor
Accept Karah Parshad with cupped hands and join the Langar

links.label: Read about Gurdwara conduct in the Rehat Maryada

lessons.title: Amrit Sanchar
lessons.summary: The Sikh initiation ceremony into the Khalsa.

sections.heading: About Amrit Sanchar
paragraphs: Amrit Sanchar is conducted by five initiated Sikhs representing the Panj Pyare, in the presence of the Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. Amrit is prepared in an iron bowl, stirred with a Khanda while Banis are recited.
Initiates commit to keeping the Five Ks, reciting Nitnem and following the Sikh code of conduct. Anyone ready to accept this discipline may take Amrit, whatever their background.

links.label: Amrit Sanchar in the Rehat Maryada

lessons.title: Sikh Rehat
lessons.summary: The Sikh way of life and code of conduct.

sections.heading: About Rehat
paragraphs: Rehat is the discipline of Sikh life. The Sikh Rehat Maryada, published by the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee (SGPC), sets out personal conduct, Panthic conventions and ceremonies.

lessons.title: Kesh
lessons.summary: Uncut hair, kept in the form the Creator gave.

sections.heading: Meaning
paragraphs: Kesh is uncut hair, kept as a sign of accepting the Creator's will and the natural form given by the Creator.

sections.heading: Importance
paragraphs: Kesh is central to Sikh identity. It is covered with a Dastar (turban) or head covering, which also signals a commitment to stand up for others.

sections.heading: Historical context
paragraphs: Keeping uncut hair was practised by the Gurus and given as an article of faith to the Khalsa in 1699. Dishonouring the hair is one of the four cardinal prohibitions for initiated Sikhs.

sections.heading: In simple words
paragraphs: Sikhs don't cut their hair because they accept themselves as the Creator made them.

lessons.title: Kangha
lessons.summary: A small wooden comb kept in the hair.

sections.heading: Meaning
paragraphs: The Kangha is a small wooden comb kept in the hair.

sections.heading: Importance
paragraphs: It keeps the Kesh clean and tidy, and symbolises an orderly, disciplined life of body and mind.

sections.heading: Historical context
paragraphs: Given to the Khalsa in 1699, the Kangha reflects the Gurus' teaching that spiritual life does not mean neglecting the body, as some ascetics of the time did.

sections.heading: In simple words
paragraphs: Sikhs comb their hair twice a day, as a reminder to keep both body and mind clean.

lessons.title: Kara
lessons.summary: A steel or iron bracelet worn on the wrist.

sections.heading: Meaning
paragraphs: The Kara is a plain circle of steel or iron worn on the wrist.

sections.heading: Importance
paragraphs: Its circle — without beginning or end — reminds a Sikh of the eternal Creator and of the bond with the Guru. Seen on the hand, it is a reminder to act rightly.

sections.heading: Historical context
paragraphs: The Kara was given to the Khalsa as an article of faith in 1699. It is plain rather than decorative, reflecting simplicity.

sections.heading: In simple words
paragraphs: The Kara is a reminder on your hand: before you do something, ask whether the Guru would approve.

lessons.title: Kachera
lessons.summary: A cotton undergarment.

sections.heading: Meaning
paragraphs: The Kachera is a specific style of cotton undergarment.

sections.heading: Importance
paragraphs: It symbolises self-control, modesty and faithfulness, and was practical clothing allowing free movement.

sections.heading: Historical context
paragraphs: Given to the Khalsa in 1699, the Kachera suited a people who needed to be ready at all times — in contrast to the loose garments of the period.

sections.heading: In simple words
paragraphs: The Kachera reminds Sikhs to be modest and in control of their desires.

lessons.title: Kirpan
lessons.summary: An article of faith in the form of a sword.

sections.heading: Meaning
paragraphs: The Kirpan is an article of faith in the form of a small sword. Its name is often explained as joining kirpa (mercy) and aan (honour).

sections.heading: Importance
paragraphs: It represents the duty to protect the weak, stand against injustice and uphold dignity. It is a religious article, not a weapon of aggression.

sections.heading: Historical context
paragraphs: Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji's Miri Piri swords and Guru Gobind Singh Ji's creation of the Khalsa established the ideal of the saint-soldier (Sant Sipahi), symbolised by the Kirpan.

sections.heading: In simple words
paragraphs: The Kirpan reminds Sikhs to be brave and to protect anyone who is being treated unfairly.

lessons.title: The creation of the Khalsa (1699)
lessons.summary: How Guru Gobind Singh Ji created the Khalsa on Vaisakhi 1699.

sections.heading: Vaisakhi 1699
paragraphs: At Anandpur Sahib, Guru Gobind Singh Ji asked the gathered Sangat who would offer their head for their faith. Five Sikhs from different regions and castes came forward — remembered as the Panj Pyare.
The Guru initiated them with Khande di Pahul (Amrit), then asked them to initiate him in turn, showing the equality of Guru and disciple. Thus the Khalsa was born.

links.label: See it on the history timeline

lessons.title: The Guru Granth Sahib as Guru (1708)
lessons.summary: How the scripture became the eternal Guru of the Sikhs.

sections.heading: From Adi Granth to Guru Granth
paragraphs: Guru Arjan Dev Ji compiled the Adi Granth and installed it at Sri Harmandir Sahib in 1604. Guru Gobind Singh Ji added the Bani of Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji, and at Nanded in 1708 declared the Granth the Guru for all time.
Since then Sikhs have bowed before the Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji as their living Guru.

lessons.title: The Five Takhts
lessons.summary: The five seats of Sikh temporal authority.

sections.heading: The Takhts
list: Sri Akal Takht Sahib, Amritsar — established by Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji in 1606
Takht Sri Kesgarh Sahib, Anandpur Sahib — birthplace of the Khalsa
Takht Sri Damdama Sahib, Talwandi Sabo — linked to the final recension of the Guru Granth Sahib
Takht Sri Patna Sahib, Bihar — birthplace of Guru Gobind Singh Ji
Takht Sri Hazur Sahib, Nanded — where Guruship passed to the Guru Granth Sahib Ji

gurus.name: Guru Nanak Dev Ji
gurus.birthplace: Rai Bhoi di Talwandi (Nankana Sahib, present-day Pakistan)
gurus.bio: Guru Nanak Dev Ji was born to Mehta Kalu and Mata Tripta. From childhood he questioned empty ritual and caste. After a profound spiritual experience at Sultanpur Lodhi he travelled for many years — journeys known as the Udasis — sharing a message of One Creator, truthful living and the equality of all people. In his later years he settled at Kartarpur, where the Sikh way of life of Kirtan, honest farming and a shared kitchen took shape.
contributions: Founded the Sikh faith and its core teachings
Composed Japji Sahib and many shabads in the Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji
Established Sangat (congregation) and Langar (community kitchen) as lived equality
Travelled widely in dialogue with people of many faiths

events.text: Born at Rai Bhoi di Talwandi
Spiritual revelation at the Kali Bein, Sultanpur Lodhi
The Udasis — long journeys with Bhai Mardana
Settles at Kartarpur on the banks of the Ravi
Passes Guruship to Bhai Lehna (Guru Angad Dev Ji)

teachings: Ik Onkar — there is One Creator
Naam Japna, Kirat Karni and Vand Chhakna
No one is high or low by birth

gurus.name: Guru Angad Dev Ji
gurus.bio: Born Bhai Lehna, he became a devoted follower of Guru Nanak Dev Ji, whose humility and service led Guru Nanak to name him Angad — “a part of my own body”. From Khadur Sahib he strengthened the young community, giving shape to its institutions so the Guru's message could spread and endure.
contributions: Standardised and popularised the Gurmukhi script
Collected and preserved Guru Nanak Dev Ji's Bani
Expanded the Langar, run with great dedication by his wife Mata Khivi Ji
Encouraged physical fitness alongside spiritual discipline

events.text: Passes Guruship to Guru Amar Das Ji

gurus.name: Guru Amar Das Ji
gurus.bio: Guru Amar Das Ji became Guru in his seventies after years of tireless service to Guru Angad Dev Ji. From Goindwal Sahib he organised the growing Sikh community and made equality visible: everyone, whatever their status, first sat together in the Langar.
contributions: Made sitting together in the Langar central to meeting the Guru
Established the Manji system to organise Sikh congregations
Spoke against sati and the seclusion of women
Built the Baoli Sahib (step-well) at Goindwal and composed Anand Sahib

events.text: Passes Guruship to Guru Ram Das Ji

gurus.name: Guru Ram Das Ji
gurus.bio: Born Bhai Jetha, he served Guru Amar Das Ji with deep devotion and married Bibi Bhani, the Guru's daughter. As Guru he founded the town of Ramdaspur, which grew into the city of Amritsar, and composed the four Laavan sung at every Sikh wedding.
contributions: Founded Ramdaspur (Amritsar) and began excavating its sacred pool
Composed the Laavan of the Anand Karaj
Encouraged traders and craftspeople to settle in the new town

events.text: Passes Guruship to Guru Arjan Dev Ji

teachings: Married life as a spiritual path

gurus.name: Guru Arjan Dev Ji
gurus.bio: The youngest son of Guru Ram Das Ji, Guru Arjan Dev Ji completed Sri Harmandir Sahib, with doors on all four sides as a sign that it is open to everyone. He compiled the Adi Granth, bringing together the Bani of the Gurus and of saints from different backgrounds. He was the first Sikh martyr, executed at Lahore in 1606.
contributions: Built Sri Harmandir Sahib (the Golden Temple)
Compiled the Adi Granth (1604), with Bhai Gurdas Ji as scribe
Composed Sukhmani Sahib and a large share of the Bani
Founded Tarn Taran and Kartarpur (Jalandhar)

events.text: Installs the Adi Granth at Sri Harmandir Sahib

gurus.name: Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji
gurus.bio: After his father's martyrdom, Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji wore two swords — Miri (temporal authority) and Piri (spiritual authority) — and built the Akal Takht facing Sri Harmandir Sahib. He trained Sikhs to defend themselves and was later held at Gwalior Fort; his release is remembered as Bandi Chhor Divas.
contributions: Established the Akal Takht (1606)
Introduced the principle of Miri Piri
Organised the Sikhs to defend themselves against injustice

events.text: Becomes the sixth Guru; Akal Takht established
Passes Guruship to Guru Har Rai Ji

teachings: Balance of spiritual and worldly duty
Courage in defence of the oppressed

gurus.name: Guru Har Rai Ji
gurus.bio: The grandson of Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji, Guru Har Rai Ji was known for his gentleness and compassion for all living things. At Kiratpur Sahib he maintained gardens and a dispensary of herbal medicine; Sikh tradition records that he sent medicine even to the son of the Mughal emperor.
contributions: Maintained a herbal dispensary open to all
Kept a trained body of Sikh horsemen while avoiding conflict
Continued missionary work across the region

events.text: Passes Guruship to Guru Har Krishan Ji

gurus.name: Guru Har Krishan Ji
gurus.bio: Guru Har Krishan Ji became Guru at the age of five. Summoned to Delhi, he served people suffering from a smallpox epidemic without regard to their faith. Gurdwara Bangla Sahib now stands where he stayed. Before passing, he indicated that the next Guru would be found at Bakala.
contributions: Served and healed the sick during an epidemic in Delhi
Showed that wisdom does not depend on age

events.text: Passes away in Delhi, naming “Baba Bakale” as successor

gurus.name: Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji
gurus.bio: The youngest son of Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji, he was found in deep meditation at Bakala and became the ninth Guru. He founded Chak Nanki (Anandpur Sahib) and travelled widely. When Kashmiri Pandits sought his help against forced conversion, he gave his life in Delhi in 1675 for the freedom of others to practise their faith — honoured as Hind di Chadar, the “Shield of India”.
contributions: Founded Anandpur Sahib (1665)
Composed shabads and Saloks included in the Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji
Gave his life defending religious freedom

events.text: Becomes the ninth Guru at Bakala

gurus.name: Guru Gobind Singh Ji
gurus.bio: Guru Gobind Singh Ji became Guru at nine after his father's martyrdom. A poet, scholar and warrior, he created the Khalsa on Vaisakhi 1699 at Anandpur Sahib. He faced great hardship — his four sons and his mother were martyred — yet remained in Chardi Kala. In 1708 at Nanded he declared the Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji the eternal Guru.
contributions: Created the Khalsa and gave the Five Ks (1699)
Composed Jaap Sahib, Tav-Prasad Savaiye, Benti Chaupai and other works
Prepared the final recension of the Guru Granth Sahib at Damdama Sahib
Conferred eternal Guruship on the Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji (1708)

events.text: Creates the Khalsa at Anandpur Sahib
Battle of Chamkaur; martyrdom of the Sahibzade
Guruship passes to the Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji at Nanded

teachings: Sovereignty and equality of the Khalsa
The Guru Granth and the Guru Panth
